teaching.mainQuestion: How can bread mould start growing on another piece of bread?
teaching.learnerAction: Trace the visible structure that produces spores, explain how spores can move to a new food surface, and explain how a landed spore can establish new fungal growth.
teaching.structure: Causal mechanism followed by an unseen spatial application. Observation of an existing mould colony comes before microscopic vocabulary or reproductive classification.
teaching.entryCheck: Recall in one sentence that reproduction produces new individuals. The picture establishes that this is a fungus on bread, not a seed or a flowering plant.

scenes.narration: You may have seen a fuzzy patch spreading across old bread. That patch is a fungus. But how could it start growing on another piece of bread without the two pieces touching? Let’s follow one example, a bread mould called Rhizopus stolonifer.
scenes.visualBrief: Bread and mould fill the main area, with the learner question in clear negative space. Cut to an identified named-organism illustration linked to the colony. No definition list or sexual/asexual badge.

scenes.purpose: Connect the visible patch to the organism's body
scenes.narration: Close up, the mould is made of thin branching threads. One thread is called a hypha; several are hyphae. These threads grow over and into the bread. The fungus gets nutrients from the bread, which support its growth. The fuzzy patch is a growing fungal body, rather than a pile of loose spores.
scenes.visualBrief: Whole fungal colony, then one anchored magnified region where threads meet bread. Label 'Hyphae: fungal threads'. Keep enough bread to explain location. Do not introduce mycelium, septa or chromosome structures.
scenes.visualReuseDecision: New verified anatomical illustration; retain same colony identity.
scenes.purposefulCue: Magnify at 'thin branching threads'; highlight the food contact at 'nutrients from the bread'.
scenes.hold: Stable view while the causal food-to-growth sentence is spoken.

scenes.purpose: Locate the structure that produces reproductive cells
scenes.narration: Some threads form upright stalks with rounded heads. Inside a head, the fungus produces many tiny reproductive cells called spores. A spore can begin new fungal growth. The rounded structure where these spores form is called a sporangium. So the sporangium makes the spores; the spores are the cells that can begin a new fungus.
scenes.visualBrief: First show the stalk in its colony, then select one sporangium and a consistent cutaway detail containing spores. Two physical labels: 'Sporangium' and 'Spores'. The contained cells must be visibly distinct from the enclosing structure.
scenes.visualReuseDecision: New source-checked cutaway, not a flow node.
scenes.purposefulCue: Select the head at 'rounded heads', then reveal the inside detail at 'Inside'. Name the term after the plain explanation.
scenes.hold: Allow the structure/cell distinction to settle before release.

scenes.narration: When the sporangium matures, its wall breaks down and spores can be released. Air movement can carry them away from the parent mould. This allows a spore to reach another food surface, even when no fungal thread joins the two places. Arriving is only the first step. The spore still needs conditions that allow it to grow.
scenes.visualBrief: Source-backed release stage, then a selected spore on a separated bread surface. Keep the earlier colony as useful orientation, not repeated paragraphs. A few illustrated spores indicate movement rather than measured particle counts.
scenes.visualReuseDecision: New separate release/arrival states; existing leader/reveal code may direct attention.
scenes.purposefulCue: Release at 'wall breaks down', movement at 'Air movement', stable arrival at 'first step'.
scenes.hold: Hold the landed spore before presenting germination; no immediate mature colony jump.

scenes.purpose: Explain why a landed spore may establish a new fungal body
scenes.narration: On suitable food, with enough moisture and a suitable temperature, the spore can begin to grow. We call that germination. A thin thread grows out from the spore, then branches to build a new fungal body. In the production route we have shown, the parent mould made the spores without reproductive cells joining. That is asexual reproduction. Rhizopus also has a sexual route, so finding a spore on its own would not tell us how it was produced.
scenes.visualBrief: Accurate germinating spore with an emerging thread, followed by a small branching colony. Bring in 'Germination: beginning to grow' after its plain meaning. State the asexual conclusion only after the sequence. A final short boundary sentence replaces the earlier detail; no sexual-cycle diagram now.
scenes.visualReuseDecision: New anatomical stage artwork or reviewed model. Same bread and spore identity across states.
scenes.purposefulCue: Conditions stay available while the thread emerges. Name germination after the causal growth condition. Classification arrives at its spoken sentence, not during an earlier attempt.
scenes.hold: Stable completed sequence with only the current small colony and needed food/moisture condition.

scenes.purpose: Unseen spatial application without classification words supplied as the answer
scenes.narration: Here is a new situation. Piece A has a mature Rhizopus colony. Piece B starts as sterile, moist bread. The pieces do not touch, but they share moving air. Both are kept at a temperature suitable for this mould. Explain how mould from A could establish a new colony on B. Include how it could travel and what would grow after it arrives. Take a moment to work through that sequence.

scenes.purpose: Reason through travel and establishment in separate stages
scenes.narration: The bread pieces do not need to touch. Mature sporangia on A can release spores, and moving air can carry some towards B. If a spore lands on B, the moist bread supplies water and nutrients. At the stated suitable temperature, it can germinate: a fungal thread begins to grow, then branches into a new colony. The possibility depends on a spore arriving and growing. Sharing air does not guarantee that every piece of bread will develop mould.

Demonstrate physical fungal structure and causal growth before expanding the full lesson. Do not include yeast, meiosis, chromosome sets or the full practice question in this first visual pilot.
immediateMouldPilot.narration: This bread has a fuzzy patch of mould. How could it start growing on another piece of bread? Let’s follow a bread mould called Rhizopus. Close up, its body is made of thin branching threads called hyphae. They grow over and into the bread, taking up nutrients that support growth. Some threads form upright stalks with rounded heads. Inside a head, the fungus makes spores: tiny reproductive cells that can begin new fungal growth. The head is called a sporangium. When its wall breaks down, spores can escape. Moving air can carry them to another piece of bread. If a spore finds enough moisture, food and a suitable temperature, a thread can grow out from it and branch into a new fungal body. That beginning of growth is germination. The production route we have shown is asexual. Rhizopus also has a sexual route, so a spore alone does not identify how it was produced.
